q: What type of psychological test is the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS)?

concept.t: The WAIS samples broad reasoning, knowledge, working memory and speed, and combines them into a Full Scale IQ.
Pooling many abilities into one overall score is the job of an intelligence test (Section 9.1).

wrong.a: Predicts how well someone will learn one specific skill with training, as the Differential Aptitude Tests do; the WAIS measures broad ability instead.
wrong.c: Measures an evaluative stance towards an object, which is a Social book topic, not a cognitive test.
wrong.d: Measures what a known course of teaching has already produced, as a board examination does.

q: Which of the following technique/process involved in guidance is called "the heart of the guidance programme"?
who: Aptitude testing in educational and career guidance

concept.t: Aptitude tests forecast how well a person will learn a course or an occupation.
Guidance decisions about which stream or career to choose rest on that forecast, so the key gives aptitude testing this title.
Be aware that the standard textbook phrase is "counselling is the heart of the guidance programme". Counselling is not offered here, but if it appears as an option, choose it.

wrong.a: Also a guidance tool, but an intensive life history that describes the person's past and present rather than predicting future learning.
wrong.b: Also a guidance tool, but a face-to-face conversation that describes the person's present rather than predicting future learning.
wrong.c: Also a guidance tool, but a running school file of past and present records rather than a forecast of future learning.

q: Which of the following psychologists is associated with the development of the first intelligence test?

concept.t: Alfred Binet and Théodore Simon published the first practical intelligence scale in 1905 (Section 9.2).
It had 30 items of increasing difficulty and was built to pick out Paris schoolchildren who needed special teaching.

wrong.a: Freud founded psychoanalysis and had nothing to do with intelligence testing.
wrong.b: The bait: Piaget worked in Simon's Paris laboratory around 1920 standardising reasoning tests, but children's errors led him to a theory of cognitive development, not the first test.
wrong.d: Skinner is the figure of operant conditioning and had nothing to do with intelligence testing.

q: The term IQ was invented by

concept.t: William Stern proposed the Intelligenzquotient in 1912: mental age divided by chronological age.
Terman later multiplied Stern's quotient by 100 and made the IQ famous through the 1916 Stanford-Binet, but he did not coin it.

wrong.a: The tempting wrong answer: Terman multiplied Stern's quotient by 100 and made the IQ famous through the 1916 Stanford-Binet, but did not coin it.
wrong.b: Allport is a trait theorist of personality; he never worked on the IQ.
wrong.d: Watson is the founder of behaviourism; he never worked on the IQ.

q: IQ if any body has a mental age of 8 and a chronological age of 10 is:

concept.t: Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, where MA is mental age and CA is chronological age.
A quick check: whenever mental age is below chronological age, the IQ must be below 100.

wrong.a: Not produced by any calculation with these numbers; it is also above 100, which is impossible when MA is below CA.
wrong.b: The commonest slip: turning the ratio upside down (10 ÷ 8 × 100 = 125).
wrong.d: Not produced by any calculation with these numbers; the correct working gives 80.

q: To determine whether a newly developed intelligence test truly accurately measures intelligence or not, it is necessary to administer the test with one that has been in the field for some time. Which of the following needs to be looked for?

concept.t: Giving the new test together with an established test and correlating the two sets of scores.
That is criterion-related validity with the criterion measured at the same time, that is, concurrent validity (Section 9.3).

wrong.a: The broader question of whether the test behaves as the theory of intelligence predicts across many kinds of evidence, not one correlation.
wrong.c: Judged by examining whether the items sample the domain, not by correlating with another test.
wrong.d: Also criterion-related, but needs a criterion gathered later, such as next year's grades.

q: In the WAIS-IV (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition), how many core subtests are there in the Verbal Comprehension Index and the Perceptual Reasoning Index respectively?

concept.t: The Verbal Comprehension Index core is Similarities, Vocabulary and Information: 3 subtests.
The Perceptual Reasoning Index core is Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Visual Puzzles: 3 subtests (Table 9.5).

The options with a 4 are tempting because each index also has supplemental subtests (Comprehension for VCI; Picture Completion and Figure Weights for PRI), but these only substitute for core ones and do not count towards the core total of 10.

wrong.a: Counts a supplemental PRI subtest (Picture Completion or Figure Weights) as core; the PRI core is only 3.
wrong.c: Counts the supplemental Comprehension subtest as core VCI; the VCI core is only 3.
wrong.d: Undercounts the VCI, whose core is 3, and adds a supplemental subtest to the PRI's core of 3.

q: Which of the following subtests is part of the core battery for the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS-IV) but NOT typically found in the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-V)?

concept.t: Digit Span, Symbol Search and Matrix Reasoning are primary subtests in both the WAIS-IV and the WISC-V, so none of them can be the answer.
Letter-Number Sequencing is the only option that is not a primary WISC-V subtest; it is a secondary one there.
Strictly, it is a supplemental, not core, subtest of the WAIS-IV (it was core in the WAIS-III), so the stem is loose, but (d) is clearly the best of the four.

wrong.a: A primary Working Memory subtest in both the WAIS-IV and the WISC-V, so it does not separate the two.
wrong.b: A primary Processing Speed subtest in both the WAIS-IV and the WISC-V, so it does not separate the two.
wrong.c: Primary in both: part of Perceptual Reasoning in the WAIS-IV and Fluid Reasoning in the WISC-V.

q: What is the age range valid for Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, 5th edition (WISC-V)?

concept.t: The WISC-V covers 6 years to 16 years 11 months.
It fills the gap between the WPPSI-IV, which ends at 7 years 7 months, and the WAIS-IV, which begins at 16 years (Table 9.4).

wrong.a: Matches no Wechsler scale; the WISC-V starts at 6 and runs to 16 years 11 months.
wrong.c: Moves the lower end up by a year; the WISC-V starts at 6 years.
wrong.d: Moves the upper end down by a year; the WISC-V runs to 16 years 11 months.

q: Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) is primarily designed to measure which type of intelligence?

concept.t: Each item requires working out the rule behind a novel pattern of figures, with almost no language or learned knowledge.
Solving a new problem without leaning on learned knowledge is fluid reasoning (Sections 9.3 and 9.4).

wrong.a: Acquired knowledge, measured by vocabulary and information subtests; crystallised intelligence is what the matrices avoid.
wrong.c: Exactly what a non-verbal test like the RPM avoids.
wrong.d: Thorndike's ability to understand and manage people; the matrices do not sample it at all.

q: Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM) measure which kind of intelligence?
who: Raven's SPM (1938), classic measure of Gf

concept.t: The SPM (1938) is the classic measure of Gf, fluid intelligence.
Raven's is also the best single marker of Spearman's g, and Gf and g are closely related; but when fluid intelligence is offered, it is the more precise and expected answer.

wrong.a: Acquired knowledge, which is precisely what the matrices were designed to keep out.
wrong.c: Fails because crystallised knowledge is precisely what the matrices were designed to keep out, so only half of it is true.
wrong.d: The tempting one: Raven's is the best single marker of Spearman's g, but with fluid intelligence offered, Gf is the more precise answer.

q: A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias?

concept.t: Its five performance subtests (Kohs blocks, pass-along, pattern drawing, immediate memory, picture construction) need no reading.
It has Indian rural norms (Section 9.3), so an unschooled rural child is compared with a fair reference group.

wrong.b: Leans heavily on school-built verbal knowledge and was normed on other populations, not Indian rural children.
wrong.c: Like the WISC, the SB5 leans heavily on school-built verbal knowledge and was normed on other populations.
wrong.d: The tempting Indian option, but half of MISIC is verbal, adapted from the WISC's information, comprehension, arithmetic and vocabulary items.

q: The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale can be used to assess eligibility for:
who: WAIS Full Scale IQ plus adaptive behaviour (Section 9.3)

concept.t: A WAIS Full Scale IQ, together with a measure of adaptive behaviour, documents intellectual disability or acquired cognitive impairment.
That evidence supports a disability certificate or allowance (Clinical link, Section 9.3).

wrong.a: Depends on income and need, not on cognitive ability.
wrong.c: Assessed by clinical interview and specific risk scales, not by an intelligence test.
wrong.d: The tempting option, but it concerns children, who are assessed with the WISC or an Indian equivalent rather than the adult scale.

q: Cattell considered crystallised intelligence to be a (an)
who: Cattell, crystallised intelligence (Gc) as invested ability

concept.t: Gc is what fluid ability has "invested" in and crystallised through education and experience.
Vocabulary, general knowledge and learned methods: a repertoire of information, skills and strategies (Section 9.4).

wrong.a: Gc does develop, but "a development process" describes how it grows, not what it is.
wrong.b: The classic swap: this is the definition of fluid intelligence, not crystallised.
wrong.d: Far from it: crystallised abilities such as vocabulary are the ones that hold up best with ageing.

q: According to the Guilford model of intelligence, how many dimensions of intelligence are there?

concept.t: Guilford's cube crosses 5 operations × 4 contents × 6 products = 120 separate abilities (1967), later 150 and then 180 (Section 9.4).
The key uses "dimensions" loosely to mean the cells. Strictly, the cube itself has three dimensions (operations, contents and products), so on a literal reading (a) is the correct fact.
The paper's key nevertheless went to 120, so for this exact question mark (b); whenever a question asks how many abilities or factors, choose 120.

wrong.a: Literally true, as the cube's three dimensions are operations, contents and products; but the key counted the 120 cells, so it loses here.
wrong.c: No basis in the model: ten matches none of Guilford's counts (3 dimensions; 120, 150 or 180 abilities).
wrong.d: No basis in the model; the number of abilities is fixed by the cube, not by a person's IQ.

q: Which type of intelligence according to Sternberg's Triarchic theory of intelligence includes the ability to easily adapt to the present environment or select a more favourable environment than the existing one or modify the environment to fit one's need?

concept.t: Adapting to, selecting and shaping (modifying) the environment are the three functions of the contextual subtheory.
Sternberg later called this ability practical intelligence (Section 9.5).

wrong.a: The analytical machinery of metacomponents, performance and knowledge-acquisition components, not dealing with the environment.
wrong.c: Belongs to Dweck's incremental (growth) theory of intelligence, not to Sternberg's triarchic theory.
wrong.d: A corruption of experiential, the subtheory of coping with novelty and automatising, that is, creative intelligence.

q: Individual differences in intelligence are due to:
who: Twin and adoption studies, gene-environment interaction (Section 9.7)

concept.t: Twin and adoption studies show substantial heritability, but it is well below 1 and varies with age and circumstances.
Nutrition, schooling, adoption, early intervention and the Flynn effect show large environmental effects.
Genes and environment interact, so only a many-factor answer fits (Section 9.7).

wrong.a: Ignores half the evidence: the large environmental effects of schooling, nutrition and the Flynn effect.
wrong.b: Ignores half the evidence: the substantial heritability shown by twin and adoption studies.
wrong.c: Names only one environmental factor, socio-economic status, leaving out schooling, nutrition, family environment and the rest.

q: The cardinal DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criterion for Mental Retardation is based primarily on an IQ score:

concept.t: With a mean of 100 and an SD of 15, two SDs below the mean is an IQ of about 70.
About 70 is the DSM-IV-TR cut-off for significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (Section 9.8).

wrong.a: Would be an IQ of about −5, which does not exist on the scale.
wrong.b: An IQ of 85, which is merely low average, not disability.
wrong.d: An IQ of 40, which already lies at the moderate to severe boundary, far below the cut-off.

q: In which of the following situations would a diagnosis of "global developmental delay" be inappropriate?
who: DSM-5 global developmental delay, under age 5 (Section 9.8)

concept.t: Global developmental delay is a provisional DSM-5 diagnosis for children under 5 whose severity cannot yet be assessed reliably (Section 9.8).
The 7-year-old is over 5 and has been fully assessed, with both intellectual and adaptive deficits documented, so he receives a diagnosis of intellectual disability itself.

wrong.a: Fits the label: an assessment not yet possible at this age is exactly what the provisional label exists for.
wrong.c: Fits the label: the assessment is incomplete (adaptive skills unknown), exactly the situation the provisional label exists for.
wrong.d: Fits the label: the assessment is incomplete (cognitive level not measured), exactly the situation the provisional label exists for.

q: Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) is a measure of:

concept.t: Doll's VSMS (1935) converts social competence into a social age.
SQ = (SA ÷ CA) × 100 (Section 9.8).

wrong.a: These come from intelligence tests (mental age and IQ), not from a social maturity scale.
wrong.c: These come from infant scales such as Gesell's and Bayley's, which give the DQ, not from the VSMS.
wrong.d: Not a standard pairing: "emotional age" is not a standard measure, and EQ is Bar-On's emotional quotient, unrelated to the VSMS.

q: In Terman's study of gifted children, social and behavioural problems were found only in those with:
who: Terman's gifted study; Hollingworth, Children Above 180 IQ

concept.t: As a group, Terman's "Termites" were healthier and better adjusted than average.
The problems that did occur were concentrated among those whose childhood IQs were about 180 or more, in line with Hollingworth's Children Above 180 IQ (Section 9.8).

wrong.a: Cannot be right, because 150 is about the average of the whole gifted group.
wrong.b: Right threshold, but omits the key point that the IQs were childhood scores.
wrong.c: Wrongly places the testing in adulthood; the scores of 180 or more were childhood scores.

q: Which of the following disabilities is explicitly covered under the scope of The National Trust Act (1999) in India for the welfare of persons with the disability?

concept.t: The Act's full title names its four groups: autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation and multiple disabilities (Indian context, Section 9.8).
Autism and intellectual disability (mental retardation) are both named, so (d) is the full answer.

wrong.a: Named in the Act, but choosing it alone misses the other named group, mental retardation.
wrong.b: Not among the four; it is recognised under the broader Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
wrong.c: Named in the Act, but choosing it alone misses the other named group, autism.
